lines.text: To see why this was remarkable, start with the problem.
Earth and Mars both circle the Sun, at different speeds. So the distance between them keeps changing, from about fifty-five million kilometres to around four hundred million.
You can't fly straight there. You launch onto a long, curving path around the Sun, and aim for where Mars will be, months later.
Even on the best path, the trip takes many months. Mangalyaan's took about ten.
The planets line up for this only once every twenty-six months. Miss the window, and you wait more than two years.
And getting there is only half the battle. Over the decades, many missions to Mars have failed. Some on launch, some on the way, some in the final minutes.
Until then, India had only ever been as far as the Moon.
Even the space powers struggled at first.
The Soviet Union's first two Mars probes, in 1960, never even reached orbit.
America's first attempt, Mariner three, failed in 1964, when its protective cover wouldn't open.
Japan's Nozomi never managed to enter Mars orbit, in 2003. China's first Mars orbiter was lost in 2011, along with the Russian probe that was carrying it.
Reaching Mars on the first try was almost unheard of.
On the third of August, 2012, the Indian government approved the mission.
The next launch window would open in November 2013.
That left about fifteen months to build a spacecraft that could survive a journey to another planet.
Trick one: a smaller rocket.
ISRO's most powerful rocket at the time, the GSLV, had failed twice in 2010. So they chose the smaller, reliable PSLV.
On the fifth of November, 2013, it lifted off from Sriharikota.
But the PSLV wasn't powerful enough to throw the spacecraft straight to Mars. It could only put it into a long, oval orbit around Earth.
So ISRO used a clever trick. Every time the spacecraft swung closest to Earth, where it moves fastest, it fired its engine.
Engineers call this the Oberth effect. A push given where you're already moving fastest adds the most energy.
Each burn stretched the orbit wider. Over about a month, a series of burns pushed its highest point out beyond a hundred thousand kilometres.
Then, on the first of December, one final burn flung it free of Earth, and onto the road to Mars.
Trick two: keep it small.
At launch it weighed about thirteen hundred and forty kilograms, and most of that, about eight hundred and fifty, was fuel.
Mangalyaan carried just five science instruments. Together, they weighed about fifteen kilograms.
A camera to photograph the planet. Sensors to study its atmosphere, and to hunt for methane.
And its structure and engines were similar to India's first Moon probe, Chandrayaan-one. Proven designs meant less new engineering, and less to pay for.
Trick three is people.
A large share of any space mission's cost is salaries. And engineers in India earn a fraction of what they would in the United States or Europe.
And nearly everything was designed and built in India, avoiding expensive imports.
A small team, a tight schedule, and no time for extras.
Not everything went to plan.
On the eleventh of November, 2013, during the fourth orbit-raising burn, the main engine shut down early. A valve fault had cut off its fuel.
Engineers planned an extra burn to make up the difference, and the spacecraft got back on track.
Then came the long cruise. For about three hundred days, the main engine sat unused, in the cold of deep space.
Would it fire again when it mattered most?
On the twenty-second of September, 2014, two days before arrival, ISRO tested it, for just four seconds. It worked.
Two days later came the burn you saw at the start. Twenty-four minutes, in Mars's shadow, entirely on its own.
Mangalyaan wasn't alone. That same week, NASA's MAVEN orbiter also reached Mars.
A bigger spacecraft, with more instruments, and a budget of several hundred million dollars.
Both worked. One cost a fraction of the other.
Mangalyaan was designed to last six months.
It kept working for about eight years.
It photographed the whole planet, and its moon, Phobos, and studied the Martian atmosphere.
India was so proud of it that Mangalyaan later appeared on the back of the two-thousand-rupee banknote.
Contact was finally lost in 2022, when its fuel ran out and its batteries drained.
Spread over a journey of roughly six hundred and fifty million kilometres, Prime Minister Modi pointed out, the trip cost about seven rupees per kilometre.
Less than an auto-rickshaw ride.
So cheap didn't mean careless.
It meant choosing simple, proven solutions, and letting physics do the work that money usually does.
Nine years later, the same frugal approach helped Chandrayaan-three land near the Moon's south pole, the first mission ever to land there.
That's how India reached Mars for less than the cost of a movie, and got there on its very first try.
